seo.title: Karmic tail 6 5 17 compatibility: two lights in one house
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 5 17 compatibility: The Lovers, The Hierophant and The Star — how love passes through other people's rules and learns to let two lights shine.

title: The 6-5-17 karmic tail in compatibility: love, rules and two lights under one roof
short: The 6-5-17 karmic tail in compatibility reads like a novel with the ending in the wrong place. First The Lovers, then The Hierophant — the card of the teacher, the rite and the rules — and only after them, in the place of the main task, The Star. An ordinary love story ends with the wedding. For a 6-5-17 couple the main thing begins the next morning: how two people, each with a light of their own, can live under one roof without putting each other out.

sections.h2: The main card comes after the wedding
paragraphs: The most famous love story in music is usually told up to a single date. On 12 September 1840, in the church at Schönefeld near Leipzig, Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck were married — after three years of secret engagement, her father's ban and a lawsuit against him. That is usually where the story stops.

What happened the next day is more interesting. On 13 September Clara turned twenty-one, and Robert gave his wife a notebook, making the first entry himself. It was to be a diary of everything that touched their household and married life, he wrote — "a book of the requests which we have to make of each other, when words fail to express our meaning", and a book of reconciliation if they ever misunderstood each other. They would write in turn, a week each, and hand the book over every Sunday. Anyone who wrote less than a page in a week would receive a punishment to be devised later. At the end came three words, as a talisman: industry, frugality and loyalty. Under his name Clara wrote: "Your wife, who is devoted to you with her whole heart, Clara."

The Lovers, The Hierophant, The Star — their story went in exactly that order. A declaration made in a language understood by one person in the hall. A book of rules — first her father's, then their own. And a question that neither the court nor the wedding could settle: how two talents can live in one house. In 1840 the public knew Clara Wieck's name better than her husband's: she had been playing at the Leipzig Gewandhaus since the age of nine, while many people took his originality for immaturity.

The Schumanns are not presented here as "a couple with the 6-5-17 tail": the calculator does not work with dates before 1900, and dates are not the point. Their story is a plot in which this tail can be read from the first card to the last — and from documents: letters, diaries, a court ruling.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a declaration played in public
paragraphs: The point "Entry to the task" shows what the couple want together, what they have agreed on, which "common language" they speak. Lisovskaya places this point on the line of tasks, which makes it double-edged: the very wish that started the union can later turn into resistance.

For the Schumanns the common language was literally music. For a year and a half Clara's father kept them from seeing or writing to each other. On 13 August 1837 Clara gave a morning concert in Leipzig and put Robert's F-sharp minor sonata on the programme — the one published without his name, "dedicated to Clara by Florestan and Eusebius", his two invented alter egos. Later she explained: "I played because I knew no other means of showing you what was in my heart. I could not do it secretly, so I did it in public." That same day Robert wrote her his first letter in eighteen months: "Are you still firm and true?" — and asked for a simple "yes".

This is the six at the entry in its purest form: choosing each other against everyone, and a language in which something said before a full hall is heard by one person. Three years later, on the eve of the wedding, Robert gave his bride the song cycle Myrthen (Myrtles). Its first song, "Widmung" (Dedication), to a poem by Rückert, is about a love that makes a person dearer to himself: "That you love me makes me worthy in my own eyes… Lovingly you lift me above myself" (our translation). There is no better formula for the entry to this tail: love as the first mirror in which each of them likes what they see.

That mirror has a reverse side. If your love is what gives me my worth, then without it I am worth nothing, and the shared wish "for things between us to be beautiful, chosen, true" turns into a test. Lisovskaya describes the minus of the six as two kinds of couple: the noisy one, with jealousy and daily showdowns, and the closed one, where nobody speaks about what matters. In life these are often the same two people: in company they finish each other's sentences, at home every small thing becomes an exam on "do you still love me?". A common language easily becomes a field that has to be divided. That is exactly what happened to the Schumanns: the music that joined them became, in marriage, the subject of a quiet dispute — over silence, over hours at the piano, over the right to be heard.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a book someone else writes for you
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own: it is an "addition" to the main task. In our reading it is the path — what the couple does and goes through between the wish and the task. For 6-5-17 the path runs through The Hierophant. Benebell Wen says the card "is about the pedagogy of wisdom and divine knowledge" and describes someone who "relies on another, a figure of authority or an institution, to define for the Seeker what is right and wrong".

The Schumanns had one Hierophant between them: Friedrich Wieck, Clara's father and the teacher of both. In 1830 Robert moved into his house as a pupil. Wieck taught his daughter from early childhood and kept her diary for her. The first page of her first diary bears, in her father's hand, the words: "My diary, begun by my Father, May 7 1827, and to be continued by Clara Josephine Wieck." The first volume is almost entirely his — written in her voice. In the autumn of 1828 nine-year-old Clara reports "herself" that her father has noticed again that she is "still lazy, careless, disorderly, obstinate, and disobedient". Her biographer Berthold Litzmann, who worked with all forty-seven volumes of her diaries, remarks that until the summer of 1838 they reflect "not her thoughts and opinions, but her father's".

Wen has a sentence about The Hierophant that describes Wieck completely: one may shield another person from knowledge with the best of intentions, but the result will be negative, because "We are not the keeper of others." In June 1836, on her father's orders, Clara sent Robert back all his letters. Then came the court: the couple asked for permission to marry without her father's consent. At the hearing on 18 December 1839 Wieck was so passionate that "the President of the court had to call him to order", and Clara wrote that the day had torn to pieces "the tender bond between father and child". The ruling came on 1 August 1840. The Hierophant in this story is doubled: one law held the couple back, another set them free.

The most interesting part is what became of the book of rules after the wedding. The couple did not abolish The Hierophant; they replaced him. The marriage diary is the father's diary again, except that now two people are supposed to write it, in turn. Litzmann calls Robert's rules the laws of an "order of matrimony" and notes straight away that "the lawgiver himself was the chief offender". Carried away by composing, Robert wrote less and less, then stopped, and after the Russian tour of 1844 the book stayed with Clara alone. A written dialogue about "questions which they hesitated to discuss by word of mouth in the bustle of the day" became a monologue again.

The teacher stayed in the house too — only now he was the husband. In the second week of their marriage they worked through The Well-Tempered Clavier together. Clara wrote: "Robert scolded me sharply; I had been doubling a passage in octaves, and so had added a fifth voice, incompatible with four-part writing." In the same book, where she praises Mendelssohn's fugues, Robert added an objection in the margin — the names of three other masters. A fifth voice that has no place in someone else's order is a coincidence, but an exact one: the middle of this tail is a five, and it is the five that tests whether the shared order has room for one more voice.

The quietest Hierophant lived in Clara herself. In November 1839 she wrote: "I once thought that I possessed creative talent, but I have given up this idea; a woman must not desire to compose — not one has been able to do it, and why should I expect to? It would be arrogance." Here "the way things are done" speaks in her own voice and calls the dream arrogance — the very word that opens Waite's list for The Star reversed.

In a 6-5-17 couple the middle of the task is easy to recognise without the nineteenth century. Whose family decides how to celebrate, how to spend, how to bring up children. A parent's voice that suddenly comes out of the partner's mouth. One partner teaching the other — how to dress, speak, work — and sure of knowing better. The constant glance at "what will people say". Among the tasks of the five Lisovskaya names interference from relatives, attempts to remake each other, and a shared decision about the family that has to be reached without lecturing. Rules are not the enemy in themselves: in its plus The Hierophant is trust, loyalty, shared views, the traditions a home rests on. The question of the middle is a different one — whose rules they are, and who holds the pen.

sections.h2: Main task: two pianos that may not sound at once
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mostly through the minus: what does not work for the couple and what they have to learn. For 6-5-17 it is The Star — the card of a light that can be seen.

There were two grand pianos in the Schumanns' house, but they were not both allowed to be heard at the same time: the walls were thin, and Robert was composing. In January 1841 Clara wrote: "My playing is getting all behindhand, as is always the case when Robert is composing. I cannot find one little hour in the day for myself!" Robert saw it. At the end of 1840 he wrote: "For too often she has to buy my songs at the price of silence and invisibility." And he added: "So must it be in an artist's life, and if two people love each other, it is right enough."

Silence and invisibility is an exact definition of The Star in the minus: the light is there, but it has been put out so as not to disturb the other. Among this card's tasks Lisovskaya names the fear of fulfilling one's own dream and the habit of getting in the way of the partner's. In the Schumann house both halves lived under one roof, and without any ill will at all.

Then came the mirror scene. In February 1842, on tour, an invitation arrived from the court of Oldenburg — for Clara alone. She went and came back pleased. Robert wrote that "the thought of my undignified position in such cases, prevented me from feeling any pleasure". A few weeks later they parted: Clara went on to give concerts in Copenhagen, while he returned to their little daughter and his journal. On 14 March Robert left in their shared book the most honest lines of their marriage: "The separation has once more made me very conscious of my peculiar and difficult position. Am I to neglect my own talent, in order to serve you as a companion on your journeys? Have you allowed your talent to lie useless, or ought you to do so, because I am chained to the paper and to the piano? […] But what will the world say? Thus I torture myself with thinking. Yes, it is most necessary that we should find some means by which we can both utilise and develop our talents side by side."

The whole tail is in one paragraph. "A companion on your journeys" — the partner as an entourage. "What will the world say?" — The Hierophant who has moved into one's head. "Our talents side by side" — a formula for the main task that could not be bettered.

Even the biographer speaks in the voice of the tail's middle. Litzmann calls the young Clara Wieck a "girl-priestess" who, "like the star which shines out of a purer atmosphere, and in quiet silent beauty sheds its light abroad" — and at once explains that when such gifts are weighed against each other, the husband's creative power must outweigh the wife's interpretive one, and that Clara, as he puts it, realised "it was at once her highest duty and her highest happiness to lose herself in him". The Star and The Hierophant in a single paragraph: the light is acknowledged, but the order decides whom it is for.

The Star also has a quiet form of the minus — comparison. In 1846 Clara wrote a piano trio, her largest work. At the first rehearsal she was delighted: "There is nothing greater than the joy of composing something oneself, and then listening to it." And in the same entry: "of course it is only a woman's work, which is always lacking in force, and here and there in invention." A year later, when the printed copies came, she set her trio beside Robert's, and "after Robert's (D minor), it sounded effeminate and sentimental". In her recommendations to a couple with this tail Lisovskaya advises moving away from comparing oneself with one's partner and with other couples. Clara was not comparing her husband with someone else; she was comparing herself with her husband — and losing before the game began.

Her trio is Op. 17. Under the same number Robert has the Fantasie in C major; on 18 March 1838 he wrote to his bride that its first movement was "a deep lament for you". This is a coincidence, not evidence, but the picture is exact: under one number, a light directed at a beloved person, and one's own light, which its owner judged weak.

In a modern couple this card is recognised without any notes. One partner's success becomes the union's shop window, and the other turns into the "plus one" on the invitations. One is too shy to say what they want and backs this with sensible reasons; the other, meaning well, talks the partner out of a risky dream. The partner is compared with exes, with other couples, with who they "ought to be". The photos together are lovely — and not a word has been said about what matters. In her analysis of this tail Lisovskaya names what is perhaps the sorest point: much is left unsaid, especially about feelings, and resentment and jealousy grow out of what is unsaid. If mockery and pressure in the couple have become constant and it feels frightening to be near the partner, this is no longer a question for the cards: it calls for a psychologist, and if there is a threat, for a local emergency number or crisis line.

sections.h2: Clues in Waite: open to each other, the Hierophant's sign, the Star's two ewers
paragraphs: The pictures of the Waite–Smith deck lay out the same story in three frames. This is about his cards: the cards on the site are drawn differently in places.

On The Lovers Waite sees a man and a woman "unveiled before each other" and calls it "in all simplicity the card of human love". Before each other, not before the world: this is the couple's entry, their language for two.

The Hierophant gives a sign with his right hand which, according to Waite, is "distinguishing between the manifest and concealed part of doctrine". Two priestly ministers kneel before him. In the older decks, Waite recalls, the card was "called also Spiritual Father". The one who decides for two people what to show and what to hide — for the Schumanns this was a father in the most literal sense.

"For the majority of prepared minds," Waite writes, the figure of The Star "will appear as the type of Truth unveiled". From "unveiled before each other", through "what to show and what to hide", to a truth that is open to everyone — that is how the couple's openness changes along the tail. And one more detail: "She pours Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land." One figure, two streams. In the language of a couple The Star demands what Robert wrote about: two channels for two talents, not one into which everything is poured.

Wen adds two sentences to this line. Her Hierophant is someone who relies on an authority to define what is right. Of The Star she writes: "Guidance is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within." That is the whole path from the middle of the tail to its task: from someone else's voice deciding who gets to shine, to one's own. And one more of her observations: "Unlike Temperance, where there is a balancing between the levels of awareness, The Star card depicts a pouring out in one direction." For a couple this is a warning: if one only shines and the other only receives the light, The Star turns into service.
The 6-5-17 tail is not rare: one couple in 28 has it (3.539%), fifth place among the 97 couple tails. A great many couples live through the plot "love — rules — star".

**Neither of the two owns the couple's Star.** The seventeen in the couple's main task is always an exact sum of the two personal karmic tasks, with no reduction: 7 + 10, 5 + 12, 6 + 11, 4 + 13, 8 + 9. So the partners in such a couple never have The Star as their personal karmic task, and in a personal tail it appears in only 16% of these couples — in the partner whose tail is 6-17-11, and even then in the middle. The main card of the tail is a shared light, assembled from two different tasks and belonging to neither. The question "which of us is the star" is put wrongly from the very start.

**The couple does not bring this story with them.** The tail is formed by eight combinations of personal tails. In almost half of the couples (45%) it is one and the same combination: 12-19-7 in one partner and 21-4-10 in the other; next come 15-20-5 + 18-3-12 (24%) and 18-6-6 + 6-17-11 (16%). In 50.5% of the couples neither partner has The Lovers, The Hierophant or The Star in their personal tail. The tail arises between the two — just as the Schumanns' question of "talents side by side" could not have arisen for either of them alone.

**The couple's rules are made of its love and its star.** The middle of a couple's tail is counted from the two personal middles, and it always comes out by reduction: the sum is 23, and 2 + 3 = 5 (most often 19 + 4). But this tail has another coincidence: the entry and the main task together also give the middle, 6 + 17 = 23 → 5. And in 16% of the couples The Hierophant is literally assembled from one partner's Lovers and the other's Star — the personal middles of the tails 18-6-6 and 6-17-11. Our reading: the couple's book of rules is written from what the two of them love and from what each of them wants to shine with.

**The couple is built like one person.** The centre of the couple's matrix in these couples is only ever of two kinds: The Tower (16) in 74% and The Chariot (7) in 26%. With both, the formula of a personal matrix holds — "main task plus centre gives the entry": 17 + 16 = 33 → 6 and 17 + 7 = 24 → 6. Arithmetically a 6-5-17 couple looks like one person with this tail, but it is read differently — more on that below.

**An example from the book.** The only couple on which Lisovskaya demonstrates a full consultation in her book is a couple with this tail. She writes it from the end to the beginning, 17-5-6, and calls it the couple's "karmic programme". That couple's centre is also The Tower, and the partners' personal tails are the same 12-19-7 and 21-4-10 as in the example below.

sections.h2: How the 6-5-17 tail comes about: an example with 05.07.1975 and 14.10.1975
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added.

ul: **05.07.1975.** Day 5, month 7, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task 5 + 7 + 22 = 34 → 7, centre 5 + 7 + 22 + 7 = 41 → 5, entry to the tail 7 + 5 = 12, middle 7 + 12 = 19. Personal tail: 12-19-7.

paragraphs: The couple's tail is assembled from these two tails point by point:

The middle of a couple's tail is counted only from the two personal middles. Here the sum of the couple's outer numbers also gives 5, but that is a property of this particular tail, not a way of calculating.

In this couple The Star stands in two more places: in the point "What to create together" (birth months 7 + 10 = 17), which Lisovskaya reads only in the plus, and in the point "Parents together". One card is both the couple's main trial and what they are meant to create together. Lisovskaya suggests adding up repeats: 17 + 17 + 17 = 51 → 6 — The Lovers, the card of the entry. The couple's centre is 5 + 11 = 16, The Tower; "The couple's values" is 12, The Hanged Man.

sections.h2: The Tower, The Chariot and the couple's values
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is "The atmosphere inside the couple" — what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In three couples out of four with this tail it holds The Tower. In the plus Lisovskaya describes it as a union that goes through any trial hand in hand, in which the partners see and bring out each other's potential. In the minus — the collapse of an invented image of the partner. For a couple whose task is The Star, this is one theme seen from two sides: the image the other is made to fit will sooner or later fall, and it is well if what falls is the image and not the union. Her analysis of a couple with this tail and The Tower in the centre also contains an everyday warning: in such an atmosphere what is said in the heat of the moment stays in the memory for a long time. And in money matters The Tower in the plus means strict order by rules the two have invented together; the Schumanns' book with its laws is exactly such an attempt.

Every fourth couple has The Chariot in the centre. Then the atmosphere is movement: each has their own development outside the family, and what matters, according to Lisovskaya, is to walk side by side but each on their own road. Its minus is rivalry for leadership and the demand that the partner give up their goals for someone else's. Robert's question — whether he should neglect his own talent to become his wife's companion on her journeys — is The Chariot asking The Star.

"The couple's values" answer what the union exists for. In half of these couples (50.4%) it is The World — a whole in which everyone has a place; in the plus Lisovskaya writes of full acceptance of the partner and of rules created together, in the minus of re-educating the other to suit oneself and mocking their plans. In 28.6% it is The Hanged Man: in the plus, the care of one partner who does everything for the other; in the minus, sacrifice "because that's how it must be" and a lovely picture outside with heaviness inside. In 21% it is The Empress: home, children, creation, and yet each must have their own fulfilment, while the minus is contempt for the one who has "fallen behind" in growth. Our reading: in all three variants the couple's values come up against the same fork as the tail — a union is valuable when both grow in it, not one at the other's expense.
The tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast: it is a theme the couple will live through one way or another. The script is changed not by promises but by a few quite ordinary decisions.

ul: **Writing its own book of rules.** Not living by the statutes of the parental families and "the way things are done", but agreeing on its own: holidays, money, whose time is when. Lisovskaya advises a couple with a five to create their own holidays and places and to get on with relatives without letting them inside the couple's borders.

**Keeping a book of requests.** For the Schumanns it was a notebook for what is hard to say aloud. A 6-5-17 couple needs its own channel for what goes unsaid — a note, an agreed weekly conversation — as long as it is regular and for the two of them, not only after a quarrel.

**Giving the second piano its hours.** If there are two talents in the house, each needs their own hours and their own place, not the leftovers of someone else's schedule. "Our talents side by side" is a timetable, not a slogan.
**Not measuring oneself by the partner.** Comparison is the quiet form of The Star's minus. It was not a critic who called Clara's trio "only a woman's work", but a voice in her own head.
**Not putting out another's light out of care.** Talking a partner out of a dream "for their own good" is exactly the guardianship Wen means: we are not the keeper of others.

**Not living for show.** Lisovskaya advises this couple not to put their relationship on display and not to share everything intimate. A lovely picture for others is The Star's minus; a light that the two of them see is its plus.

sections.h2: The strong version: songs with no composer's name
paragraphs: The best thing the Schumanns did with this tail fits into one songbook. In the winter of 1841 Robert took up the idea of publishing songs together with his wife, chose poems from Rückert's Liebesfrühling (Love's Spring) for her, and wrote nine songs himself in a week. Clara could not get anywhere; she wrote: "I have no talent at all for composing." Then in the first week of June she wrote four songs and gave them to her husband for his birthday. Three went into the joint volume — twelve songs under a double number: Robert's Op. 37 and Clara's Op. 12. Which song was whose, the edition did not say. Robert gave Clara the first printed copy on 13 September 1841 — her birthday and the anniversary of their shared book. Rückert answered them both with a poem.

One of Clara's songs in this volume is "Liebst du um Schönheit", and its text reads like an exam on the tail's main task: "If thou lovest for beauty, O love not me: love the sun with her golden hair. If thou lovest for youth, O love not me: love the spring, which is young every year. If thou lovest for treasure, O love not me: love the mermaid, she has many pearls. If thou lovest for love, O yes, love me" (our translation). The Star in the minus is love for a picture: for beauty, youth, status, for how the couple looks from outside. The Star in the plus is when people love the one who shines, not the light.

Sixty years later Gustav Mahler set the same poem — for his wife Alma, whom shortly before their wedding he had asked to give up composing: there would be one composer in their house. One poem and two marriages. In one, the wife writes the song, and her name stands on the cover next to her husband's. In the other, the song is written for a wife who is not supposed to compose. Between them lies exactly the difference between a Hierophant the couple wrote themselves and a Hierophant handed to them.

The end of the Schumanns' story has nothing to do with the tail: the cards do not predict events. But one scene from the last years of their marriage is worth telling. At the end of 1853, on a triumphant tour of Holland, Clara played at a soirée given by a prince. Afterwards their host asked Robert: "Are you musical, too?" — and, hearing "yes", went on: "And what instrument do you play?" Litzmann writes that in earlier years this would have hurt Robert deeply, but now he only smiled. This is The Star lived to the end: a light that no longer needs to be recognised at court.

After Robert's death in 1856 Clara lived another forty years. She wrote almost nothing more for the public, but to the end of her life she played his music and prepared the complete edition of his works. She had done the same before: in May 1844 in Moscow, at a matinée for thirty or forty listeners, she played his piano quintet, which could not be performed at the big concert because of the size of the hall. A Star that pours water on her own land and on someone else's.

sections.h2: The 6-5-17 tail in a couple and in one person
paragraphs: The same three numbers also occur as a personal tail — on 818 dates since 1900. But that is a different calculation with different roles for the points: a personal tail describes one person's programme, a couple's tail describes a task that arises between two people and that neither of them has alone. Readings of one cannot be carried over to the other, even when the numbers are the same.

These numbers do not occur in any other order in a couple. A couple's entry to the task is always a multiple of three, so 17-5-6 or 5-6-17 will not appear in a couple's matrix. Lisovskaya's 17-5-6 is the same tail, read from the main task back to the entry.

ul: The Schumanns' diaries and letters — from Berthold Litzmann's biography Clara Schumann: ein Künstlerleben nach Tagebüchern und Briefen (1902–1908), in Grace E. Hadow's English translation, Clara Schumann: An Artist's Life (1913).
Robert's letter of 18 March 1838 about the Fantasie — from the preface to the Henle edition.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot; Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015).
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024).
Friedrich Rückert's poems "Widmung" and "Liebst du um Schönheit" — our translation.
**Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** Where the couple starts and what they want together: to choose each other and to speak a language only the two of them understand.
**Middle of the task — 5, The Hierophant.** How the couple moves on: through rules — first other people's (parents, teachers, "the way things are done"), then rules they write themselves.
**Main task — 17, The Star.** What the couple learns: to let both of them shine — without turning the union into a shop window, the partner into an audience, or one's own dream into a sacrifice.

faq.q: What does the 6-5-17 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, running from The Lovers through The Hierophant to The Star. The couple enters it by choosing each other and finding a common language, passes through rules — first other people's, then their own — and the main thing they learn is to let both of them shine: without a shop window, without comparisons, and without one going dark for the sake of the other.

faq.q: Is the 6-5-17 tail bad for a couple?
faq.a: No. It is neither a verdict nor a forecast but a theme of the union, and the tail is common — one couple in 28 has it. The main task is read through the minus because it shows where the couple has to learn; in the plus the same Star is a union in which each, beside the other, understands who they want to be.

faq.q: Which partner is responsible for The Star?
faq.a: Neither alone. The Star in the couple's main task is always an exact sum of the two personal karmic tasks, and neither partner has it as a personal task. There is no point looking for whose light it is: it appears only when the two are together.

faq.q: Why does Lisovskaya write this tail as 17-5-6?
faq.a: Lisovskaya writes a tail from the main task to the entry, while the site writes it from the entry to the main task. Her 17-5-6 and the site's 6-5-17 are one and the same couple tail. These numbers do not occur in any other order in a couple: a couple's entry to the task is always a multiple of three.

report: The 6-5-17 couple tail reads like a novel with the ending in the wrong place: the wedding sits in the middle. First The Lovers, then The Hierophant — the card of the teacher, the rite and the rules — and only after them, in the place of the main task, The Star. An ordinary love story ends at the altar. For this couple the main thing begins the next morning: how two people, each with a light of their own, can live under one roof without putting each other out.

The most famous couple in the history of music lived this plot, and left the documents. On 12 September 1840 Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck were married — after three years of secret engagement, her father's ban and a lawsuit against him. On 13 September Robert gave his wife a notebook, a diary for two: "a book of the requests which we have to make of each other, when words fail to express our meaning". They would write in turn, a week each. The Schumanns are not "a couple with the 6-5-17 tail" — theirs is a plot in which the tail can be read from the first card to the last.

report.h3: A declaration in a language for one

report: The entry to the task is The Lovers: what the couple want together and which common language they speak. For the Schumanns that language was music. When her father forbade them to meet, Clara put Robert's sonata on her concert programme and later explained: "I could not do it secretly, so I did it in public." Something said before a full hall was heard by one person.

Such an entry has a reverse side. The shared wish "for things between us to be beautiful, chosen, true" easily turns into a test, and the common language into a field that has to be divided. The music that joined the Schumanns became, in marriage, the subject of a quiet dispute — over silence, over hours at the piano, over the right to be heard.

report.h3: A book of rules in someone else's hand

report: The middle of the task is The Hierophant, the path through rules. The Schumanns' first Hierophant was Clara's father, the teacher of both. Her childhood diary opens in his hand: "My diary, begun by my Father, May 7 1827, and to be continued by Clara Josephine Wieck." He wrote almost the whole first volume in her voice: nine-year-old Clara reports "herself" that she is "still lazy, careless, disorderly, obstinate, and disobedient".

The marriage diary is the father's diary again, except that now two people are supposed to write it. That is the movement of the tail's middle: from someone else's book of rules to one's own. But the quietest Hierophant lived in Clara herself. In November 1839, before the wedding, she wrote: "a woman must not desire to compose — not one has been able to do it, and why should I expect to? It would be arrogance." Here "the way things are done" speaks in her own voice and calls the dream arrogance. In a modern couple this is a parent's voice coming out of the partner's mouth, one partner's habit of teaching the other, and the constant glance at "what will people say". **The question of the middle is not whether rules are needed, but who holds the pen.**

The main task is The Star, the card of a light that can be seen, and it is read through the minus. There were two grand pianos in the Schumanns' house, but they were not both allowed to be heard at the same time: Robert was composing. He himself wrote that too often his wife had **"to buy my songs at the price of silence and invisibility"**. The light is there, but it has been put out so as not to disturb the other — and without any ill will at all.

Then came the mirror scene: an invitation arrived from the court of Oldenburg for Clara alone, and Robert wrote of his "undignified position". A few weeks later, when Clara went on to give concerts in Copenhagen, he left the most honest lines of their marriage in the shared book, asking whether he was to neglect his own talent in order to serve as her companion on her journeys, and whether her talent was to lie useless because he was "chained to the paper and to the piano". "But what will the world say?" And the conclusion: **"it is most necessary that we should find some means by which we can both utilise and develop our talents side by side"**. The whole tail is in one paragraph: the partner as an entourage, The Hierophant in one's head, and a formula for the main task.

The Star also has a quiet form of the minus — comparison. Of her own trio Clara said: "of course it is only a woman's work", and beside Robert's trio it "sounded effeminate and sentimental". She was not comparing her husband with someone else; she was comparing herself with her husband — and losing before the game began. In a modern couple this card is recognised without any notes: one partner's success becomes the union's shop window, the other becomes the "plus one" on the invitations, the partner is talked out of a dream "for their own good", and not a word has been said about what matters, especially about feelings.

report.h3: A light that belongs to neither

report: The numbers of this tail hold a clue: the seventeen in the couple's main task is always assembled from the two personal karmic tasks, and neither partner has The Star as a personal task. **The question "which of us is the star" is put wrongly from the very start** — this light appears only when the two are together. In Waite the figure of The Star "pours Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land": two channels for two talents, not one into which everything is poured. Wen writes of The Star: "Guidance is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within."

The script is changed by quite ordinary decisions: writing one's own book of rules instead of the statutes of the parental families; keeping a book of requests for what goes unsaid, rather than waiting for a quarrel; giving the second piano its own hours, not the leftovers of someone else's schedule; not measuring oneself by the partner; not putting out another's dream out of care.

The best thing the Schumanns did with this tail is a joint songbook to poems by Rückert: twelve songs under a double number, and which song was whose, the edition did not say. One of Clara's songs is "Liebst du um Schönheit": "If thou lovest for beauty, O love not me… If thou lovest for love, O yes, love me." The Star in the minus is love for a picture. The Star in the plus is when people love the one who shines, not the light. Years later, on a tour of Holland, a prince who had heard Clara play asked Robert whether he was musical too, and on hearing "yes", which instrument he played. Robert only smiled. This is The Star lived to the end: a light that no longer needs to be recognised at court.
